title: BIT Data Type
description: Learn how to use the BIT data type to store bit values (0, 1, or NULL) in SQL Server.

data.text: The BIT data type is an integer data type that can take a value of 0, 1, or NULL. SQL Server optimizes storage of BIT columns.
If a table has 8 or fewer BIT columns, SQL Server stores them as 1 byte. If a table has 9 to 16 BIT columns, SQL Server stores them as 2 bytes, and so on.

data.title: Create BIT Column
data.content: Creates a table with a BIT column.

data.title: Insert BIT Values

data.text: SQL Server converts string values: TRUE to 1, FALSE to 0. Any nonzero value is converted to 1.

data.title: String to BIT Conversion

data.text: A `BIT` column is true (1), false (0), or unknown (`NULL`). That third state is why `WHERE is_active = 0` silently drops rows where the value was never set. Always add `NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` when false is the sensible default.

data.title: Counting true and false values safely
data.content: T-SQL has no boolean type in the select list, so aggregate with CASE. The result shows the unknown rows explicitly.

data.title: Not standard SQL
data.text: The SQL-standard `FILTER (WHERE ...)` clause is not supported by T-SQL; `SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` is the portable substitute. Do not use bitwise operators (`&`, `|`) for ordinary true/false flags — they make queries harder to read and to index.

data.title: BIT Key Points
points: BIT stores values of 0, 1, or NULL.
SQL Server optimizes BIT column storage (1 byte for 8 or fewer columns).
TRUE converts to 1; FALSE converts to 0.
